newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian TV law seen hurting press freedom.
newsitem.headline: Colombian TV law seen hurting press freedom.

text.p: Colombia's Congress has passed a controversial law to create private television channels while increasing government control over broadcasting content.

The legislation approved late on Monday provides for the creation of three private television channels in 1998 to compete with the country's three existing state-run channels. But it also orders the government broadcasting body Inravision to review the contracts of private companies producing programmes for the state channels and empowers the National Television Commission to monitor their content.

All existing programmes from newscasts to soap operas must be submitted for the scrutiny by the five-person commission in February 1997. If the commission deems certain programmes do not meet its criteria for "objectivity and fairness" they could be taken off the air immediately.
News broadcasters denounced the legislation as a move to stifle freedom of expression and silence criticism.

While the government hailed the new law as a victory for democracy in the mass media, newscast producers saw it as revenge for their critical coverage of this year's scandal over President Ernesto Samper's ties to drug traffickers.

Directors of some of Colombia's 14 daily and weekend news shows said the law was railroaded through Congress by allies of drug barons and Samper's supporters. Samper faced a political storm over allegations that his 1994 election campaign was financed with drug cartel money, and some of the stiffest criticism came from TV news shows.

"Clearly the aim of this law is revenge. It has been pushed through by the friends of narco-traffickers in a bid to silence the TV news shows," said Maria Isabel Rueda, co-director of the respected QAP evening news programme.
But Communications Minister Saulo Arboleda insisted: "This will democratize television. It will strengthen public TV as well as creating private channels."
The law's sponsor, Sen. Bernardo Guerra, denied allegations of links to the powerful Cali drug cartel.
